title: I built a Chrome extension for the Instagram follower lists that stop halfway
title_hi: I built a Chrome extension for the Instagram follower lists that stop halfway

content:
Instagram will show a follower list, then stop. On a large account you might see a few thousand people and a spinner that never finishes. A lot of exporter extensions treat that as the end of the file.

I build IG Follower Export Tool, a Chrome extension for the way those lists behave now. Paste a profile, export followers or following to CSV or Excel, and when Instagram cuts the list off, keep going from the profiles you already have instead of saving a short file and calling it done.


  
  
  What actually breaks


The normal export walks the follower or following connection list and writes each profile to a spreadsheet. That still works on smaller accounts.

On bigger ones, Instagram often returns only part of the list. The request does not always fail. It just stops producing new people. An exporter that only paginates will sit there, or it will export a few thousand rows and look finished. The missing people were never in the response.

The extension flags that cutoff. You can save the rows you already have. Smart Capture then starts from those visible profiles and collects further accounts from them, which is the path I added because waiting on the original list does not bring the rest back.

Detailed export is separate. It adds public profile fields when Instagram shows them: bio, follower counts, and a public email or phone if the profile lists one. It is slower, and it only includes what is already on the profile.

Use a secondary Instagram account. Large exports still hit rate limits and checkpoints. The extension can pause and continue. It does not remove those limits.


  
  
  Try it before you pay


The free tier needs no subscription. Each export includes 100 profiles, or 5 profiles if you turn on detailed fields. That is enough to see the spreadsheet, the cutoff notice, and whether Smart Capture is worth it for the account you care about.

If that is all you need, stop there. You do not pay.

Pro is for unlimited exports: $9.99 a month or $79.99 a year, tied to a Google account so the plan follows you to another computer. I only want that upgrade after the free export has already been useful.

Install it from the Chrome Web Store: IG Follower Export Tool.

It runs locally in the browser you are already logged into. It is not a cloud database of leads, and it will not invent emails that a profile does not show.

title: Finally found a photo tool that stays offline
title_hi: Finally found a photo tool that stays offline
summary: I've been putting off cleaning up my photo library for way too long because every app I tried wanted to upload everythin
content:
I've been putting off cleaning up my photo library for way too long because every app I tried wanted to upload everything to the cloud first. This weekend I stumbled on Lap, a local-first open-source photo manager, and it honestly felt like a breath of fresh air. I pointed it at my messy folder of years of phone dumps and it browsed and searched everything offline, no account, no sync, nothing leaving my drive. The privacy angle isn't marketing fluff here, it's just how it works. I spent a couple of evenings tagging and deduping, and my library finally feels manageable instead of terrifying. If you've been meaning to sort out your own archive without handing it to some server, give Lap a look at https://lapphotos.com/. Small win, but a real one.

title: AI โคลนเสียงได้ใน 3 วินาที ทำยังไง?
title_hi: AI โคลนเสียงได้ใน 3 วินาที ทำยังไง?
summary:
AI โคลนเสียงได้ใน 3 วินาที ทำยังไง?

Humans now fail voice tests 25% of time — ทุกวันนี้คนเรายังแยกเสียงจริงออกจากเสีย
content:
AI โคลนเสียงได้ใน 3 วินาที ทำยังไง?

Humans now fail voice tests 25% of time — ทุกวันนี้คนเรายังแยกเสียงจริงออกจากเสียง AI ไม่ได้ถึงหนึ่งในสี่ของการทดสอบ ลองนึกภาพว่าคุณได้รับสายจากคนที่เสียงเหมือนแม่ของคุณทุกอย่าง แต่จริงๆ แล้วเป็นเสียงที่คอมพิวเตอร์สร้างขึ้นจากคลิปสั้นๆ ไม่กี่วินาที เรื่องนี้ไม่ใช่นิยายวิทยาศาสตร์อีกต่อไป และบทความนี้จะพาคุณเข้าไปดูเบื้องหลังว่ามันทำงานอย่างไร

TL;DR: AI โคลนเสียงได้จากตัวอย่างเพียง 3 วินาทีเพราะโมเดลอย่าง VALL-E ของ Microsoft เรียนรู้รูปแบบเสียงมนุษย์จากข้อมูล 60,000 ชั่วโมงมาก่อนแล้ว จึงต้องการแค่ "ลายเซ็น" ของเสียงคุณเล็กน้อย จากนั้นระบบจะแปลงข้อความเป็นสเปกโทรแกรม แล้วใช้ vocoder อย่าง WaveNet สร้างคลื่นเสียงออกมา ผลลัพธ์ดีจนผู้ฟังแยกไม่ออกในหลายสถานการณ์ และเครื่องมืออย่าง ElevenLabs ทำคะแนนคุณภาพ 0.83 เทียบเท่าเสียงมนุษย์

Key Facts ที่คนส่วนใหญ่ไม่รู้

ElevenLabs' AI in 2023 achieved 0.83 Mean Opinion Score, matching human voice quality threshold of 0.80 used by telecom industry since 1996
VALL-E by Microsoft requires only 3 seconds of voice sample to clone anyone, using 60,000 hours of LibriLight dataset with discrete codec codes
Tacotron 2 generates mel-spectrograms at 12.5ms frame intervals, then WaveNet upsamples to 24kHz using 30 dilated convolution layers with 512 residual channels


การโคลนเสียงด้วย AI คืออะไร?

การโคลนเสียงคือเทคโนโลยีที่ให้ AI เรียนรู้ลักษณะเฉพาะของเสียงคนคนหนึ่ง เช่น โทนเสียง จังหวะ และสำเนียง แล้วนำไปพูดประโยคใหม่ๆ ที่เจ้าของเสียงไม่เคยพูดมาก่อน

เปรียบเทียบง่ายๆ เหมือนนักพากย์ล้อเลียนที่ฟังคุณคุยแค่ครู่เดียวก็เลียนแบบได้ แต่ AI ทำได้เร็วกว่า ไม่เหนื่อย และทำซ้ำได้ไม่จำกัด ในอดีตระบบแบบนี้ต้องใช้การอัดเสียงหลายชั่วโมงในห้องสตูดิโอ แต่โมเดลรุ่นใหม่ลดเหลือไม่กี่วินาที

สิ่งที่ต่างจากเสียงสังเคราะห์สมัยก่อนคือ เสียงหุ่นยนต์แบบเก่าเอาเสียงสั้นๆ มาต่อกัน จึงฟังออกทันทีว่าเป็นเครื่อง ส่วนยุคนี้ AI เรียนรู้ "วิธีที่มนุษย์พูด" ทั้งหมด ไม่ได้แค่ตัดต่อ จึงได้เสียงที่ลื่นไหลและมีอารมณ์

ทำไมแค่ 3 วินาทีก็พอ?

คำตอบคือ AI ไม่ได้เรียนรู้เสียงของคุณจากศูนย์ แต่ถูกฝึกมาแล้วจากเสียงคนจำนวนมหาศาล ตัวอย่าง 3 วินาทีเป็นเพียงตัวบอกว่า "ให้พูดแนวไหน"

VALL-E by Microsoft requires only 3 seconds of voice sample to clone anyone, using 60,000 hours of LibriLight dataset with discrete codec codes โมเดลนี้มองเสียงเป็น "คำศัพท์" ชนิดหนึ่ง โดยแปลงเสียงเป็นรหัสแยกส่วน (discrete codec codes) แล้วทำนายรหัสถัดไปคล้ายที่ ChatGPT ทำนายคำถัดไป

ลองนึกถึงคนที่ฟังภาษาอังกฤษมา 60,000 ชั่วโมง พอได้ยินใครพูดสั้นๆ ก็เดาได้ว่าเขาเป็นผู้ชายหรือผู้หญิง อายุเท่าไร พูดช้าหรือเร็ว ใช้เสียงนุ่มหรือกระด้าง นั่นคือสิ่งที่ VALL-E ทำ ตัวอย่าง 3 วินาทีทำหน้าที่เป็นเหมือน "คำใบ้" ให้โมเดลดึงความรู้ที่มีอยู่มาประกอบเสียงเฉพาะตัวขึ้นมา

ElevenLabs' AI in 2023 achieved 0.83 Mean Opinion Score, matching human voice quality threshold of 0.80 used by telecom industry since 1996 — AI ผ่านเกณฑ์คุณภาพเสียงมนุษย์ที่วงการโทรคมนาคมใช้มาเกือบ 30 ปีแล้ว

เทคโนโลยีนี้ทำงานอย่างไร? 8 ขั้นตอนเบื้องหลัง

ระบบสังเคราะห์เสียงสมัยใหม่แบ่งเป็นสองช่วงใหญ่ คือ "คิดว่าเสียงควรเป็นอย่างไร" (สร้างสเปกโทรแกรม) และ "แปลงเป็นเสียงจริง" (vocoder) สถาปัตยกรรมคลาสสิกที่อธิบายได้ชัดที่สุดคือ Tacotron 2 ร่วมกับ WaveNet ซึ่งแยกได้เป็น 8 ขั้นตอน

ช่วงที่ 1: จากข้อความเป็นสเปกโทรแกรม



Text encoder: แปลงตัวอักษรที่พิมพ์เข้าไปเป็นเวกเตอร์ 512 มิติ โดยใช้การเรียนรู้ความสัมพันธ์ระหว่างตัวอักษรกับหน่วยเสียง (phoneme) เหมือนการแปลงตัวหนังสือเป็น "วิธีออกเสียง"

Attention mechanism: จับคู่ผลจาก encoder กับจังหวะของ decoder ด้วย location-sensitive attention ที่ใช้ 32 filters และ kernel กว้าง 31 ทำให้ AI รู้ว่ากำลังอ่านถึงตัวอักษรไหน ไม่ข้ามหรือพูดซ้ำ

Decoder LSTM: ใช้ 1024 units ทำนายเฟรมสเปกโทรแกรม 80 แบนด์ทีละเฟรมแบบ autoregressive คือแต่ละรอบสร้างหนึ่งเฟรม โดยดูจากเฟรมก่อนหน้า

Post-net: ใช้ convolutional layers 5 ชั้นพร้อม batch normalization ขัดเกลาผลลัพธ์และลดสิ่งแปลกปลอม (artifacts) เหมือนช่างแต่งภาพที่ลบรอยหยาบออก


สเปกโทรแกรมแบบ mel คือ "ภาพถ่ายของเสียง" ที่แสดงว่าแต่ละช่วงเวลามีพลังงานที่ความถี่ใดบ้าง ตามที่หูมนุษย์รับรู้ Tacotron 2 generates mel-spectrograms at 12.5ms frame intervals, then WaveNet upsamples to 24kHz using 30 dilated convolution layers with 512 residual channels

ช่วงที่ 2: จากสเปกโทรแกรมเป็นคลื่นเสียง



แบ่งหน้าต่าง: neural vocoder ตัดสเปกโทรแกรมเป็นหน้าต่างซ้อนทับยาว 50ms เลื่อนทีละ 12.5ms เพื่อเตรียมสังเคราะห์คลื่นเสียง

WaveNet: ส่งแต่ละหน้าต่างผ่าน gated activation layers 30 ชั้น โดย dilation rate เพิ่มแบบเอกซ์โปเนนเชียลจาก 1 ถึง 512 ทำให้มองบริบทกว้างได้โดยไม่ต้องใช้ชั้นมหาศาล

Residual และ skip: แต่ละชั้นให้ผลลัพธ์ 256 residual channels และ 256 skip channels แล้วรวม skip connections จากทั้ง 30 ชั้นเข้าด้วยกัน

ผลลัพธ์สุดท้าย: 1x1 convolution พร้อม softmax ให้ค่าแอมพลิจูดแบบ mu-law ที่ถูกแบ่งเป็น 256 ระดับ ด้วยอัตรา 24,000 ตัวอย่างต่อวินาที


ถ้าให้เปรียบ ช่วงแรกคือนักแต่งโน้ตที่เขียนว่าควรพูดอย่างไร ช่วงหลังคือนักดนตรีที่เล่นตามโน้ตออกมาเป็นเสียงจริงทีละ 24,000 จุดต่อวินาที หากอยากเข้าใจฝั่งผู้ใช้งานจริง อ่านต่อได้ที่ เบื้องหลัง ElevenLabs เสียง AI สมจริงสร้างขึ้นมาอย่างไร

ตัวอย่างในชีวิตจริงมีอะไรบ้าง?

การโคลนเสียงถูกใช้ทั้งในทางสร้างสรรค์และทางที่น่ากังวล โดยตัวอย่างที่พบบ่อยที่สุดคือการพากย์วิดีโอ หนังสือเสียง และการให้เสียงกับผู้ที่สูญเสียความสามารถในการพูด



ครีเอเตอร์: ทำพากย์เสียงคลิป YouTube หลายภาษาด้วยเสียงตัวเอง โดยไม่ต้องอัดใหม่ทุกครั้ง

ผู้ป่วย: คนที่กำลังจะสูญเสียเสียงจากโรคบางชนิดสามารถเก็บเสียงของตัวเองไว้ใช้ต่อได้

ธุรกิจ: ระบบตอบรับอัตโนมัติและสื่อการเรียนรู้ที่ฟังเป็นธรรมชาติ

มิจฉาชีพ: ปลอมเสียงญาติหรือผู้บริหารเพื่อหลอกให้โอนเงิน


เรื่องการแยกแยะ In 2024 University of Waterloo study, listeners correctly identified AI voices only 73% of the time when samples exceeded 5 seconds duration นั่นหมายความว่าแม้ฟังนานกว่า 5 วินาที ก็ยังมีโอกาสถูกหลอกกว่า 1 ใน 4

ทำไมเรื่องนี้ถึงสำคัญ?

เรื่องนี้สำคัญเพราะ "เสียง" เคยเป็นหลักฐานยืนยันตัวตนที่คนไว้ใจมากที่สุด แต่ตอนนี้ใครก็สร้างเสียงปลอมที่น่าเชื่อถือได้ด้วยต้นทุนต่ำมาก ผลกระทบครอบคลุมทั้งความปลอดภัย กฎหมายลิขสิทธิ์เสียง และความไว้วางใจในสื่อ

ข่าวดีคือยังมีร่องรอยให้จับได้ เช่น Breathing artifacts occur every 2-4 seconds in human speech but AI models before 2023 inserted breaths randomly every 8-15 seconds, creating detection pattern คือมนุษย์หายใจทุก 2-4 วินาที แต่ AI ก่อนปี 2023 ใส่เสียงหายใจแบบสุ่มทุก 8-15 วินาที ทำให้เป็นจุดสังเกตได้ อย่างไรก็ตามโมเดลรุ่นใหม่แก้ปัญหานี้ไปมากแล้ว จึงไม่ควรพึ่งวิธีนี้อย่างเดียว

วิธีป้องกันตัวที่ใช้ได้จริง ได้แก่ ตั้ง "รหัสลับ" กับคนในครอบครัว โทรกลับเบอร์เดิมเมื่อมีคนขอเงินด่วน และอย่าโพสต์คลิปเสียงยาวๆ ของตัวเองสู่สาธารณะโดยไม่จำเป็น

content:
Zero-Capital Automation: Running a Business From Termux


Okay, so you want to start a business. Cool. But the thought of upfront costs – servers, software licenses, even just a decent website – is keeping you stuck? I get it. I was there. For the last six months, I’ve been quietly building and running a (surprisingly profitable) side hustle almost entirely from my phone, using just Termux and a whole lot of scripting. And it cost me… well, almost nothing. 

This isn't about drop-shipping or affiliate marketing (though you could layer those on). This is about building automation, small tasks, and leveraging free APIs to generate income.  I’m going to break down how I do it, what tools I use, and give you some code snippets to get you started. Be warned: this isn’t point-and-click easy. It requires a willingness to learn, a bit of coding, and a whole lot of tinkering. But the reward? Genuine freedom and a business built on sweat equity, not venture capital.

What is Termux, and Why is it Awesome?

Termux is an Android terminal emulator and Linux environment.  Think of it as giving your phone a full-blown Linux command line. You can install packages, run scripts, and generally do pretty much anything you'd do on a desktop Linux system.  Crucially, it doesn't require rooting your phone.

Why is this good for business? Because you can offload tasks that would require a paid server to your phone, which you likely already own.  It’s discreet, low-power, and incredibly portable. My “server” is usually sitting in my pocket.

The Tech Stack: Keeping it Lean & Free

Here's the core of my setup:



Termux: Obviously. Get it from F-Droid (recommended for updates) or the Play Store.

Python: My scripting language of choice. Easy to learn, massive library support.  pkg install python in Termux.

Requests Library: For interacting with APIs. pkg install python-requests


SQLite: For data storage. pkg install sqlite (surprisingly powerful for small datasets!)

Cron: For scheduling tasks. pkg install cronie. This is HUGE.  It lets you automate tasks without keeping your phone screen on.

A Free API: This is the engine. I started with the SerpAPI (search engine results API - free tier is limited but useful for testing) and now use a combination of others depending on the project. Think weather APIs, currency conversion, or even data scraping (ethically, please!).

Text Editor: Termux includes nano.  Get comfortable with it.


My First Automated Business:  Local Business Data Enrichment

My first venture was surprisingly profitable.  I identified a need: a lot of small local businesses have incomplete or outdated information on online directories.  

Here's the process, and the code is simplified for clarity:



Data Source: Using the SerpAPI, I’d pull Google Maps listings for a specific city/keyword.

Data Extraction: Parse the JSON response to get business names, addresses, phone numbers, and websites.

Verification:  Compare this data against other directories (using the Requests library to scrape public websites). If there's a discrepancy, flag it.

Sales:  Contact the businesses, offering to update their listings for a small fee (typically $5-10 per business).


Here’s a snippet of Python code to get you started with the SerpAPI:



import requests
import json

def get_google_maps_results(query, api_key):
  url = "https://serpapi.com/search"
  params = {
    "engine": "google_maps",
    "q": query,
    "api_key": api_key
  }
  response = requests.get(url, params=params)
  data = json.loads(response.text)
  return data

if __name__ == "__main__":
  api_key = "YOUR_SERPAPI_KEY" # Replace with your API key
  search_query = "pizza restaurant New York"
  results = get_google_maps_results(search_query, api_key)

  if 'local_results' in results:
    for result in results['local_results']:
      print(f"Name: {result['title']}")
      print(f"Address: {result['address']}")
      # ... more data extraction here
  else:
    print("No results found.")






Automating the Process with Cron

This is where Termux shines.  I didn’t want to manually run this script every day. Enter Cron.


 Install Cronie: pkg install cronie

 Start Cronie: cronie

 Edit Crontab: crontab -e  (This opens a text editor with your cron schedule).


Add a line like this to run the script every day at 3:00 AM:



0 3 * * * python /sdcard/scripts/business_enrichment.py






Replace /sdcard/scripts/business_enrichment.py with the actual path to your Python script. Now, your phone automatically runs the script while you sleep!

Scaling & Challenges

The initial setup was slow. Scraping and data verification are CPU intensive. I improved performance by:



Optimizing the script: Using efficient data structures and minimizing API calls.

Rate Limiting:  Respecting API limits.  Implement time.sleep() to avoid getting blocked.

Data Storage: Using SQLite to cache results and avoid redundant API calls.

Rotating Proxies (advanced): If scraping is essential, consider using free proxies (be careful with security!).


Beyond Local Listings: Other Ideas

This is where the fun begins.  Here are some ideas I’ve experimented with or plan to try:



Price Tracking:  Monitor prices on e-commerce sites and alert you to drops.

Social Media Automation (Ethically!): Schedule posts using APIs, but always follow platform guidelines.

Weather Alerts:  Pull weather data and send SMS alerts for specific conditions.

Simple Data Aggregation: Combine data from multiple free APIs to create a unique dataset.


Important Considerations & Caveats



Battery Life: Automated tasks drain battery. Optimize your scripts and consider using a power bank.

Data Usage: API calls consume data. Monitor your data usage carefully.

API Limits: Free APIs have limits.  Design your scripts to handle them gracefully.

Security:  Store API keys securely. Don't commit them to public repositories.

title: When One AI Agent Is Not Enough: The Engineering Challenge of Coordinating AI Workflows
title_hi: When One AI Agent Is Not Enough: The Engineering Challenge of Coordinating AI Workflows
summary: AI agents are becoming more capable of handling multi-step tasks. But as businesses experiment with specialized agents f
content:
AI agents are becoming more capable of handling multi-step tasks. But as businesses experiment with specialized agents for research, analysis, communication, and operations, a new challenge is emerging: getting these systems to work together reliably.

Building one agent that completes a task is one problem. Coordinating several agents that share information, depend on one another, and operate under different permissions is a much larger engineering challenge.

This is where agent orchestration becomes important.

Why Businesses Are Exploring Multi-Agent Systems

A single general-purpose agent can be useful for a wide variety of tasks. However, complex business workflows often contain distinct responsibilities that require different tools, data sources, and validation rules.

Consider a business process that involves researching a request, analyzing internal data, preparing a recommendation, and updating an operational system.

A multi-agent design might assign separate responsibilities to specialized agents, with an orchestration layer controlling the sequence and movement of information.

The potential benefit is modularity: each component can be evaluated against a narrower responsibility.

But adding agents does not automatically improve performance. Every additional component introduces more interactions, possible failure points, and operational overhead.

The Difference Between Multiple Agents and a Reliable Workflow

A common mistake is assuming that agents can simply communicate with one another and produce a dependable result.

In practice, coordination requires explicit rules.

Task ownership: Each agent needs a defined responsibility and a clear boundary around what it can do.

State management: The system must know which tasks are pending, completed, blocked, or awaiting approval.

Dependency handling: A downstream action should not proceed if a required upstream result is missing or invalid.

Failure recovery: The workflow needs a defined response when an agent times out, returns an unusable result, or encounters an unavailable service.

Shared context: Agents must receive the information they need without exposing unrelated or unauthorized data.

These requirements are often more important than the number of agents in the architecture.

Why Deterministic Orchestration Still Matters

Language models are probabilistic, but important business processes often require predictable transitions.

For example, a payment-related workflow should not proceed merely because an agent produces a confident explanation. Required authorization, validation, and business rules must be satisfied independently.

A reliable architecture can combine model-driven reasoning with deterministic workflow controls.

The model can interpret unstructured input or propose the next step. The orchestration layer can check whether that step is allowed, whether prerequisites have been met, and whether a human must approve it.

This hybrid design allows flexibility where it is useful without making every critical decision dependent on generated text.

Observability Is Essential for Multi-Agent Systems

When a workflow fails, engineers need to determine whether the problem came from the model, the tools, the shared context, or the orchestration logic.

Monitoring only the final response is not enough.

A useful observability strategy records workflow transitions, tool outcomes, validation failures, retry attempts, latency, and the identity of the component responsible for each action.

Where appropriate, traces should connect related steps so engineers can reconstruct how the system reached a result. Sensitive information should be minimized or protected in logs.

Evaluation should also cover the entire workflow. An individual agent can perform well in isolation while the combined system produces incomplete or contradictory results.

Where Workflow Automation Products Fit

Businesses do not always need to build every orchestration capability from scratch. Depending on their requirements, they may evaluate workflow automation products, AI accelerators, or custom orchestration layers.

GeekyAnts' AntFlow AI is one product reference worth exploring when researching AI-enabled workflow automation and product engineering.

When assessing a solution in this space, teams should investigate how workflows are defined, how systems integrate with existing tools, how failures are handled, and how permissions and approvals are enforced. These capabilities should be confirmed against the specific product implementation and use case.

The central question is whether the solution makes a business process more reliable and manageable, rather than simply adding AI to an existing sequence of tasks.

How to Decide Whether You Need Multiple Agents

Before adopting a multi-agent architecture, ask a few practical questions:

Does the workflow contain genuinely distinct responsibilities?
Can a single agent with well-defined tools solve the problem more simply?
Do separate agents require different permissions or data access?
Can each step be evaluated independently?
Is the orchestration overhead justified by measurable improvements?

If a task is straightforward, a conventional function or deterministic workflow may be more reliable and less expensive than an agent.

Multi-agent systems are most compelling when task decomposition, specialization, and coordination provide a demonstrable benefit.

Conclusion

The next phase of agentic AI is not simply about building more autonomous agents. It is about engineering the systems that allow those agents to cooperate within reliable boundaries.

Clear responsibilities, explicit workflow states, deterministic controls, observability, and carefully defined permissions are essential to making multi-agent applications practical.

The strongest architecture is not necessarily the one with the most agents. It is the simplest architecture that can complete the required workflow reliably, recover from failures, and demonstrate measurable business value.

n8n vs Make: The Architect's Battle for Seamless Onboarding


  
  
  The Core Bottleneck & Why You Need This Stack


The harsh reality of any tech entrepreneur is waking up to a surge of API limit errors; it's the universal language of frustration. In the ruthless world of automation, time is money. The customer onboarding process is no exception, often riddled with repetitive tasks and system bottlenecks that can sap a startup’s momentum. To circumvent these challenges, choosing the right automation tool is crucial, especially when the goal is to streamline and enhance your customer onboarding workflow.

n8n and Make (formerly Integromat) emerge as significant contenders in this space, offering ways to connect disparate systems and automate workflows. But here's the brutal truth: they're not one-size-fits-all solutions. Each has its strengths and limitations, which could make or break your system's efficiency.

Streamlining onboarding processes isn't just about getting workflows automated; it's about choosing a stack that complements your business architecture and future scalability. If you're in the trenches, managing complex data flows and integrations, you'll understand how pivotal these choices are.


  
  
  Deep Dive into the Architecture (Real business scenarios)


Let me be clear, API integrations and webhook architectures form the backbone of automated onboarding systems. n8n, an open-source tool, prides itself on customizable workflows that can run on your infrastructure. Its strength lies in flexibility. You can design bespoke solutions with complete control over data privacy since it's not reliant on external servers.

Consider a SaaS startup dealing with a sudden influx of user data. n8n allows you to integrate various APIs, effectively handling data sorting, notifications, and updates across platforms with real-time precision. A typical n8n architecture might involve setting up JSON-based workflows that pull customer data, validate it against external CRM databases, and trigger conditional actions based on specific user attributes. The result? A fully automated system operating with minimal manual intervention.

Make, on the other hand, excels with its user-friendly interface, ideal for businesses needing quick setup without delving into complex code or server maintenance. With its robust pre-built templates, you can set up integrations with mainstream platforms like Slack, Shopify, and Google Workspace with just a few clicks.

In practical terms, an e-commerce business could leverage Make to automate inventory updates, customer notifications, and sales analytics by connecting their sales platform with financial systems, all in a visual, drag-and-drop environment. This setup minimizes the need for an engineering team to make frequent updates, thereby cutting costs and redirecting focus to business growth.


  
  
  Honest Pros and Cons (Brutally honest technical limits)


Let's break this down, no fluff:

n8n Pros:



High Customizability: Offers extensive room for personalized workflows.

Data Control: Host on your server for better data privacy and security.

Open Source Flexibility: Modify the code to suit your precise needs.


n8n Cons:



Technical Complexity: Requires a steep learning curve and possibly an in-house developer.

Maintenance Demand: Maintains your hosting and updates can be resource-intensive.


Make Pros:



Ease of Use: Intuitive interface with numerous pre-built templates.

Fast Deployment: Set up complex workflows quickly without technical expertise.

Scalable Infrastructure: Less worry over server load and technical debt.


Make Cons:



Limited Control: Reliance on Make's server infrastructure limits data control.

Fixed Workflows: Less flexibility for highly specific automation tasks.


Choosing between n8n and Make depends heavily on the technical bandwidth of your team and the specific requirements of your onboarding process.


  
  
  Pricing Breakdown & Automation ROI


Evaluating automation tools can't sidestep the cost discussion. Here's what it boils down to in practical terms:

n8n offers a subscription-based model and a self-hosted community version. While the community version is cost-free, the infrastructure costs bear down as your operations scale. If you're not prepared, server expenses and maintenance can escalate quickly.

Make operates on a tiered pricing model with plans scaling based on the number of operations. Its major draw is predictability in cost, leveraging cloud-computing to eliminate local server burdens. For startups aiming for rapid growth, this can mean fewer unexpected expenses.

But let’s face it: the cost isn't just about subscription fees. It's about the ROI of time saved. Automating customer onboarding reduces manual labor, allowing your team to focus on enhancing customer experiences and driving product innovation. Consider each tool's pricing in tandem with saved man-hours and operational efficiency gains.


  
  
  The Ultimate Scalability Factor


Here's a deal-breaker: scalability. As your business grows, your tech stack needs to evolve too. n8n's scalability hinges on your server capabilities. While this offers growth without third-party constraints, the technical debt can accumulate if infrastructure isn't robustly managed. 

Conversely, Make’s cloud-based model ensures system reliability with minimal concern over infrastructure load. The platform auto-scales to meet demand, liberating your team from the minutiae of server management.

Ultimately, the decision rests on your business’s growth trajectory and the technical resources at your disposal. Solopreneurs and smaller teams might lean towards Make for its ease and reliability, while tech-heavy startups could exploit n8n for its customization and ownership of infrastructure.

title: EU Digital Identity Wallets are due by 24 December 2026: what changes for apps that scan passports
title_hi: EU Digital Identity Wallets are due by 24 December 2026: what changes for apps that scan passports
summary: Originally published at EU Digital Identity Wallets are due by 24 December 2026: what changes for apps that scan passpor
content:
Originally published at EU Digital Identity Wallets are due by 24 December 2026: what changes for apps that scan passports

"EU wallets are coming at the end of 2026" has been in a lot of product roadmaps this year. If your signup or onboarding flow asks for a photo of a passport or ID card, it is worth knowing what that sentence actually means. The short version: the date is exact (24 December 2026), it binds the Member States, not you, and it does not switch off document scans.

Below: where the date comes from (with the arithmetic), what a wallet actually hands over (from the attribute tables in the rules), and a design that accepts a wallet when the user has one and falls back to a document scan when they do not.

Disclosure: this was written for the blog of doc.cheap, which reads document images. It does not read wallets, and nothing in the first half of the post depends on it.


  
  
  Where 24 December 2026 comes from


The obligation is Art. 5a(1) of Reg. (EU) No 910/2014, inserted by Reg. (EU) 2024/1183, the eIDAS amendment. Each Member State "shall provide at least one European Digital Identity Wallet within 24 months of the date of entry into force of the implementing acts referred to in paragraph 23 of this Article and in Article 5c(6)".

So the clock starts with the Commission's implementing acts, not with the amendment. The Art. 5a(23) acts are four implementing acts dated 28 November 2024, among them Implementing Reg. (EU) 2024/2979 on the integrity and core functionalities of wallets. It was published in the Official Journal on 4 December 2024, and its Art. 15 says it "shall enter into force on the twentieth day following that of its publication".




Step
Date




Published in the Official Journal
4 December 2024


Day 1 after publication
5 December 2024


Day 20 after publication: entry into force
24 December 2024


Plus 24 months (Art. 5a(1)): wallets due
24 December 2026


Plus 36 months (Art. 5f(2)): some private relying parties must accept wallets
24 December 2027




The "twentieth day following" counts from the day after publication, so it lands on the 24th, not the 23rd.


  
  
  What a wallet hands over


A wallet does not send a picture of a passport. It presents signed data. For a natural person the data set is fixed in the Annex to Implementing Reg. (EU) 2024/2977: "person identification data" (PID), issued in two formats, ISO/IEC 18013-5:2021 and the W3C "Verifiable Credentials Data Model 1.1".

Here are the attributes and their presence (Tables 1, 2 and 5 of the Annex as published on 4 December 2024), next to the nearest field in a typical passport scan response (the field names are doc.cheap's, but most scan APIs have an equivalent):




PID attribute
Presence
Nearest field in a document scan




family_name
mandatory
holder.surname


given_name
mandatory
holder.given_names


birth_date
mandatory

holder.birth_date (ISO 8601)


birth_place
mandatory
a birth_place field, when the document prints one


nationality
mandatory (alpha-2, one or more)

holder.nationality (alpha-3, one)



resident_address and the other resident_* attributes
optional
none on a passport data page


personal_administrative_number
optional
not the same thing; a document may print a personal_number



portrait
optional
the portrait image



family_name_birth, given_name_birth

optional
no curated field


sex
optional (codes 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 9)

holder.sex (M, F, X)



email_address, mobile_phone_number

optional
not on a document



expiry_date (metadata)
mandatory

document.expiry_date, but of the document, not of the PID



issuing_authority (metadata)
mandatory
an authority field, when printed



issuing_country (metadata)
mandatory (alpha-2)

document.issuing_state (alpha-3)



document_number (metadata)
optional
not the same thing: assigned by the PID provider, not the passport's number



issuing_jurisdiction, location_status (metadata)
optional
none




Three things bite when you write the mapping code:



Country codes differ. PID uses ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 (DE); passports and the machine-readable zone use alpha-3 (DEU). Keep one internal form and convert at the edge.

"Mandatory" does not mean "always known". The Annex adds that where a value "is not known for the person or cannot otherwise be issued", Member States "shall use an attribute value appropriate to the situation instead". Expect placeholders, not missing keys.

Only five attributes about the person are mandatory. Address, portrait, sex and birth names are optional. If your flow needs one of them, a given user's wallet may not carry it.



  
  
  Who still shows up with a document


The deadline obliges each Member State to provide a wallet, not anyone to use one. Art. 5a(15): "The use of European Digital Identity Wallets shall be voluntary." And: "It shall remain possible to access public and private services by other existing identification and authentication means."

So after 24 December 2026 you will still see:



Customers from outside the EU. The recitals tie the wallet to "the legal identity of Union citizens, residents in the Union or legal persons". A visitor with a passport from elsewhere has no EU wallet.

People who have not installed one, or cannot, or would rather not.

Flows that need the document itself: its image, its number or its machine-readable zone, not an attestation about the person.

The months before a given country's wallet is live. The legal deadline and the day a national wallet reaches users are different questions; the only reliable answer for one country is its own announcement or the Commission's.



  
  
  A design that takes both


Ask for a wallet presentation when the user has one, fall back to a document scan when they do not, and end both paths in the same internal record.



user starts verification
        |
        v
  offers a wallet? --yes--> wallet presentation --> verify signature --> map PID
        |                                                               |
        no                                                              v
        |                                                      internal identity
        v                                                          record
  document photo --> scan API --> map scan fields ----------------------^






Four rules keep the paths interchangeable:



One record, your own field names. Use the table above as the mapping.

Keep the source. Store whether a record came from a wallet or a scan; they carry different evidence.

Normalise empties. A scan may return null for an unknown value; a wallet may send a placeholder. Pick one convention.
Store as little as the flow needs.


Here is the fallback in Node with plain fetch, against the public sandbox key sk_sandbox_public (printed in the docs, no signup, rate limited per client address):

import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

  const response = await fetch("https://api.doc.cheap/v1/scans", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
      "Idempotency-Key": randomUUID(), // a retry returns the first result
    },
    body: JSON.stringify({
      image: readFileSync(path).toString("base64"),
      options: { retain_hours: 0, return_portrait: false }, // nothing stored
    }),
  });
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`scan failed: HTTP ${response.status}`);
  return response.json();
}

// Map a scan into the same record a wallet presentation would fill.
function fromScan(scan) {
  if (scan.meta.status !== "recognized") return null;
  const field = (name) => scan.fields.find((f) => f.id === `${name}@0`)?.value ?? null;
  return {
    source: "document_scan",
    family_name: scan.holder?.surname ?? null,
    given_name: scan.holder?.given_names ?? null,
    birth_date: scan.holder?.birth_date ?? null,
    birth_place: field("birth_place"),
    nationality_alpha3: scan.holder?.nationality ?? null,
    issuing_country_alpha3: scan.document?.issuing_state ?? null,
    document_number: scan.document?.number ?? null,
    mrz_status: scan.mrz.status, // "passed", "failed" or "absent"
  };
}






meta.status is one of recognized, no_document_found, unreadable, unsupported_document or rejected. Only the first should fill a record; the rest should send the user back to retake the photo. A passport data page carries its MRZ as two lines in the TD3 layout; the doc.cheap MRZ formats page shows TD1, TD2 and TD3 side by side.

One caveat that matters for compliance people: a scan like this is recognition. It reads what is printed and checks the MRZ check digits; the response says authenticity.overall: "not_checked". It is not forgery detection, and not the same assurance as a signed wallet presentation. If your process needs more on the scan path, it has to come from elsewhere in the flow – the doc.cheap passport OCR API comparison lists providers, including ones that do more than recognition.


  
  
  What to watch next




24 December 2026 – wallets due (Art. 5a(1)).

24 December 2027 – private relying parties. Art. 5f(2): those that must use strong user authentication for online identification, by law or by contract, "shall ... only upon the voluntary request of the user, also accept European Digital Identity Wallets". The text names transport, energy, banking, financial services, social security, health, drinking water, postal services, digital infrastructure, education and telecommunications, and excludes micro and small businesses.

Very large online platforms. Art. 5f(3) makes them accept wallets for user authentication, again on the user's voluntary request and for the minimum data needed.

Changes to the implementing acts. Recital 4 of 2024/2979 says the Commission "should review and update" it where necessary. Re-read the 2024/2977 attribute tables before you freeze a mapping.


Takeaway: build the wallet path when your users' countries ship their wallets, keep the document path, and map both into one record from day one.

This is an engineering summary, not legal advice. Is your team planning to accept the wallet, keep the scan, or both? I would like to hear how others are approaching it in the comments.

title: Building an AI Side Project That Actually Ships — Lessons from Shipping 3 MVPs
title_hi: Building an AI Side Project That Actually Ships — Lessons from Shipping 3 MVPs
summary: I remember the exact moment I almost gave up on AI side projects. I had spent three weeks building a context-aware docum
content:
I remember the exact moment I almost gave up on AI side projects. I had spent three weeks building a context-aware documentation assistant that would sit on top of my team's internal wikis. The architecture was beautiful. The prompt engineering was surgical. And after all that polish, exactly zero people used it.

That's when I realized something uncomfortable: I wasn't building products, I was building demos. The line between "working demo" and "usable product" is where most AI side projects go to die. So I changed my approach completely, and in the last two months, I've shipped three MVPs that real people actually use. Here's what I learned.


  
  
  The problem with "build something cool"


When I talk to developers about AI side projects, the pitch is always the same: "I'm building this thing that parses meeting notes and generates action items." Or "It's like Notion, but AI-native." And then they show me a beautifully designed landing page and a GitHub repo with 400 commits.

The reality is that you're competing with every other developer's midnight inspiration. The market is saturated. But worse than that, your own perfectionism is the real enemy. I've seen developers spend four weeks building a custom fine-tuning pipeline when the actual use case needed a simple fetch() call to an existing API.

My first shipped MVP in this new batch was painfully simple: a browser extension that rewrites selected text to be more concise. The entire "AI" component is a single API call wrapped in a background script. The whole thing took me a weekend. And guess what? People use it because it solves one specific problem without any friction.


  
  
  Lesson 1: The 80/20 rule is your best friend in AI


If you're building an AI feature, the model is usually the least difficult part. The hard part is everything around it: the user flow, the latency management, the error states, the UI.

Here's a concrete example. I built a small endpoint that takes a URL and returns a structured summary. The entire AI part looks like this:



from openai import OpenAI
import httpx

client = OpenAI()

def summarize_url(url: str) -> dict:
    # Fetch the content
    page = httpx.get(url, timeout=10).text

    # Truncate for context length (naive approach, works for MVPs)
    content = page[:4000]

    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4o-mini",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": "You summarize web pages into exactly 3 bullet points."},
            {"role": "user", "content": content}
        ],
        max_tokens=150
    )

    return {"summary": response.choices[0].message.content}






That's it. No RAG pipeline. No vector embeddings. No fine-tuning. For an MVP, this was enough. Users cared about the summary being fast and accurate, not about the sophistication of the retrieval process.

What I learned: The quality of your output depends less on the model and more on how well you constrain the problem. Users don't care if your solution is "AI-native" — they care if it works.


  
  
  Lesson 2: Ship the ugly version first


My second MVP was a Telegram bot that turns voice notes into organized task lists. I built it because I noticed I was sending myself voice notes at 2 AM and forgetting everything by morning.

The first iteration was ugly. No custom keyboard. No threaded conversations. It processed the voice note, sent it to Whisper, ran a prompt, and replied with bullet points. The bot's responses were formatted as plain text with dashes. My friends made fun of the UX, but they started using it.

Why? Because the core loop was solid: record → transcribe → structure → reply. Everything else was decoration.

The architecture was a simple state machine:



# Pseudocode for the bot's orchestration flow
state = "idle"

def handle_voice_message(user_id, audio):
    # Transcribe using a fast API
    text = transcribe(audio)

    # Structure the text using an LLM call
    tasks = structure_into_tasks(text)

    # Store in a simple JSON database
    save_tasks(user_id, tasks)

    # Reply with a clean list
    send_message(f"Got it! I created {len(tasks)} tasks.")






I avoided the trap of over-engineering. No Redis. No Postgres. Just a JSON file that gets backed up to S3. For 50 active users, it's more than enough. When I hit 200, I'll migrate. But the project shipped, and it ships because I let myself be embarrassed by the code for a few weeks.


  
  
  Lesson 3: You have to pick your infrastructure battles


Here's where I get honest about the backend. I have hosted models before. I've set up VLLM on a rented GPU cluster. I've spent three days getting a Docker container to play nicely with CUDA drivers. I've watched my cloud bill balloon from $20 to $150 in a single week because of a "quick" fine-tuning job.

The mistake I kept making: treating model hosting as a development problem rather than an operational problem. Owning the model means owning the GPU maintenance, the scaling issues, the cold-start latency, and the security patches. That's a job for a team whose core product is the model infrastructure. My side project is not that.

For all three MVPs, I went with pay-as-you-go API services. I don't have to think about capacity planning. When a social post goes viral and my bot gets a surge of requests, the API provider absorbs the load, and I just pay for what I use. My total API bill across all three projects? Around $12 per month. That's cheaper than a single hour of my own debugging time on a broken GPU instance.

This is what made the difference between shipping and abandoning: I stopped treating infrastructure as an engineering challenge and started treating it as a utility. I buy electricity for my apartment; I don't build a power plant. Same logic for inference.


  
  
  Lesson 4: Think about cost per user, not cost per call


A huge shift in my thinking came when I calculated my cost per active user rather than cost per request. With a $5 model like gpt-4o-mini, a daily active user costs me roughly $0.15/month in inference costs. That means even 100 active users cost $15/month. I don't need to add authentication to make it profitable. I don't need usage limits. I just need to keep building features.

This changes the entire product calculus. When the marginal cost per user is negligible, you can focus on distribution and retention. You can launch without billing. You can give your MVP away for free while you figure out if it's worth iterating on.


  
  
  The uncomfortable conclusion


After shipping three MVPs, the most shocking discovery was how little the AI part mattered. The models were all competent. The differences between them were negligible for my use cases. What made projects succeed or fail was:


How fast I could iterate on the wrapper
Whether I could handle edge cases gracefully
Whether the core experience was simple enough to explain in one sentence


One final note on AI infrastructure specifically. I went down the rabbit hole of hosting Llama 3 locally, setting up vLLM, and configuring quantization. It worked. I felt smart. And then I abandoned all of it for a hosted API because the latency was better and I didn't need to babysit a server. These days, I route most of my AI side project traffic through an aggregator that gives me access to multiple models with one key. It saves me from provider lock-in and lets me swap models mid-project without touching my code. If you're in the same boat — burning weekend hours on GPU infra instead of shipping — I'd encourage you to look at a service like tai.shadie-oneapi.com. It's a pay-as-you-go gateway that handled the model routing mess for me. One key, multiple models, zero maintenance.

The truth about side projects is that they're a test of your ability to ship, not a judgment of your AI sophistication. The developers who win are the ones who pick boring infrastructure, cut scope aggressively, and get the thing in front of users before they feel ready.

I still have a folder full of half-built AI experiments. I can't justify finishing any of them, because shipping taught me that the next idea will come faster than I think — and it will be better, because I'll know exactly where to cut corners.

Start small. Ship ugly. Let the users teach you what matters.

And for the love of everything, don't host your own model.

title: The attacker who logs in perfectly: an engineer's review of Radware's Thailand PoP launch, written for the people who sign the budget
title_hi: The attacker who logs in perfectly: an engineer's review of Radware's Thailand PoP launch, written for the people who sign the budget
summary:
Photos taken by the author at the event; slide content is Radware's.

On 8 October 2026 Radware held its Thailand PoP l
content:
Photos taken by the author at the event; slide content is Radware's.

On 8 October 2026 Radware held its Thailand PoP launch for customers and partners at the Ritz-Carlton Bangkok, under the theme "Investing in Thailand's AI and Security Transformation: Technology. Talent. Trust." I went as a network and security engineer, and I took photos of nine slides. This post is what I think those slides mean, written for executives who will never read a WAF log but do own the risk those logs describe.

Everything below comes from those slides unless I say otherwise. They are vendor material, so treat the numbers as claims, not measurements.


  
  
  The news: a new cloud security service center in Thailand






Radware announced a new cloud security service center in Thailand (its newsroom carried the release in the week of the event). On the slides, the company describes itself as 1,200 people, 40 Tbps of global mitigation capacity and more than 60 cloud security centers. I could not verify those figures independently, and the slides say nothing about how much capacity the Thai site has.

What it means for the business. Traffic cleaning closer to Thai users should mean lower latency during an attack, and it gives regulated companies a simpler answer to "where does our traffic go?". Be careful with that last point. A local scrubbing site does not automatically mean local TLS termination or local log storage. Ask the vendor those two questions in writing before you assume data residency.


  
  
  The slide that stayed with me: "The customer who logs in perfectly"




The scenario is simple. The username and password are correct. The API calls are normal. The steps happen in the right order. Every control you own says "good customer." In reality it is stolen credentials replayed at scale, a bot that has learned your app's flow, or a script that follows your process more accurately than a human would.

The slide's conclusion: signatures only catch what is already known to be bad, and only behaviour reveals bad intent.

Technical read. I agree with the direction and with a caveat. Behavioural detection is the only thing that works once the attacker holds valid credentials and rotates through residential proxies, because there is no bad signature to match. The caveat is that behavioural models produce false positives and need tuning against your own traffic. Nobody can promise you zero friction.

What it means for the business. Account takeover looks like normal revenue activity until the chargebacks and customer complaints arrive. If your fraud team and your security team look at different dashboards, this is the gap between them.


  
  
  "Nothing is broken. That's the problem."




The second slide I would show a board is about business logic abuse. Three examples were on it:


Parameter tampering: changing amount: 10 to amount: 1000 in a POST /api/transfer request that the application trusts.
Sequence abuse: skipping the Approve step in a Submit, Verify, Approve, Receive flow.
Scraping: pulling rates, offers and customer data at machine speed.


No CVE is involved, no exploit payload, no alarm. Each request is a valid API call. The slide's own summary was that a valid API is being used against you.

Technical read. This is the class of issue that scanners and signature-based WAF rules (including the OWASP Top 10 sets) tend to miss, because the request is well-formed and the flaw is in the business rule. Finding it takes someone who understands the workflow and asks what happens if a step is skipped or repeated. Runtime API behaviour analysis helps, but design review and server-side validation are still your first line.

What it means for the business. Your penetration test report can be clean and you can still lose money this way. Ask whether your last test included abuse of business flows, not only vulnerability scanning.


  
  
  Three questions Radware says every security practitioner should be able to answer





Before go-live: do you know every API and AI agent you have exposed, including shadow ones?
In production: who protects those APIs and agents while customers, apps and AI agents are using them?
Over time: how do you track behaviour and score risk as it changes?


The slide's test is that if your answer starts with "I think so," you have found a gap.

I think this is the most useful thing in the whole deck, because it costs nothing and it works on any vendor. Put these three questions to your own security lead. The honest answer to the first one is often a spreadsheet that is out of date.


  
  
  The second half: AI agents as a new attack surface








The later slides moved to what Radware calls its Agentic AI solution. As presented:


A policy enforcer that discovers, classifies, enforces and monitors AI agents.
A split between approved agents (custom-built ones, developer tools on desktops, platforms such as Teams and Slack) and unmanaged "shadow AI" (desktop apps, browser extensions).
A compliance mapping that listed the EU AI Act, GDPR, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001 and others.
A claim that agent protection must include runtime security, in two layers. At the agent level, real-time detection of misuse, prompt injection and tool abuse. At the LLM level, a configurable policy module covering prompts, data and privacy, content safety, file attachments and resource usage.
A traffic path: Internet, DDoS, firewall, WAF, bot management, LLM guardrails, then the agents with a behavioural layer.


Technical read. I like that it is drawn as an extension of the existing traffic path instead of a separate AI product. Where I am cautious: the behavioural layer for agents is the newest and least proven part, and the slides gave no detection rates or false positive figures. If you evaluate it, ask for a proof of concept on your own agents and measure it.

What it means for the business. Employees are already using AI tools that IT never approved. The risk is not the tool itself. It is that an agent can act with a person's permissions, so one successful prompt injection becomes an authorised action. You need an inventory of agents the same way you need an inventory of laptops.


  
  
  What I would do on Monday



Ask your security lead the three questions above and write down the real answers.
Ask your API owners which business flows can be skipped or repeated, and who has tested that.
Ask any vendor, Radware included, where TLS terminates and where logs are stored, in writing.
Start an inventory of AI tools and agents in use, approved or not.
If you evaluate behavioural detection, run it on your own traffic and judge the false positive rate yourself.



  
  
  Where I stand


The common thread in the event was that the attacker has already passed authentication. Defence therefore moves from "who got in" to "what are they doing now," and that needs visibility into behaviour, not just a longer rule list. That conclusion holds whichever vendor you pick.

I have not tested any of Radware's products for this post. This is a review of a presentation, not of a product.

สไลด์เปิดงาน Customer & Partner Plenary, Ritz-Carlton Bangkok, 8 ต.ค. 2026


"Radware - This Is Us": ตัวเลขบริษัทตามสไลด์ (เป็น claim ของผู้ขาย)


ภาพรวม Radware Cloud Security Services

Radware ประกาศเปิด cloud security service center ในไทย (newsroom ของบริษัทลงข่าวในสัปดาห์ของงาน) สไลด์แนะนำบริษัทว่ามีพนักงาน 1,200 คน mitigation capacity ทั่วโลก 40 Tbps และ cloud security center มากกว่า 60 แห่ง ผมตรวจตัวเลขเหล่านี้จากแหล่งอิสระไม่ได้ และสไลด์ไม่ได้บอกว่าศูนย์ในไทยมี capacity เท่าไร

ความหมายต่อธุรกิจ การ scrub traffic ใกล้ผู้ใช้ในไทยน่าจะลด latency ตอนถูกโจมตี และช่วยให้บริษัทที่อยู่ภายใต้กำกับดูแลตอบคำถาม "traffic ของเราไปที่ไหน" ได้ง่ายขึ้น แต่ต้องระวังจุดสุดท้ายนี้ การมีศูนย์ในไทยไม่ได้แปลว่า TLS termination หรือการเก็บ log จะอยู่ในไทยโดยอัตโนมัติ ให้ถามผู้ขายสองข้อนี้เป็นลายลักษณ์อักษรก่อนสรุปเรื่อง data residency


  
  
  สไลด์ที่ติดใจผมที่สุด: "The customer who logs in perfectly"



"The customer who logs in perfectly": สิ่งที่ระบบเห็น เทียบกับสิ่งที่เกิดขึ้นจริง

สถานการณ์ง่ายมาก username และ password ถูก API call ปกติ ลำดับขั้นตอนถูก ทุก control ที่มีบอกว่า "ลูกค้าดี" แต่จริงๆ คือ credential ที่ถูกขโมยมายิงซ้ำเป็นจำนวนมาก บอทที่เรียนรู้ flow ของแอป หรือสคริปต์ที่ทำตามขั้นตอนได้แม่นกว่าคนจริง

ข้อสรุปของสไลด์: signature จับได้เฉพาะของที่รู้แล้วว่าไม่ดี มีแต่ behaviour เท่านั้นที่เผย intent ที่ไม่ดี

มุมเทคนิค ผมเห็นด้วยกับทิศทาง และมีข้อแม้หนึ่งข้อ เมื่อผู้โจมตีถือ credential จริงและหมุนเวียนผ่าน residential proxy ไม่มี signature ที่ไม่ดีให้จับ behavioural detection จึงเป็นสิ่งเดียวที่ได้ผล ข้อแม้คือโมเดลแบบ behavioural มี false positive และต้องจูนกับ traffic ของตัวเอง ไม่มีใครรับประกันว่าจะไม่มีแรงเสียดทานเลย

ความหมายต่อธุรกิจ account takeover หน้าตาเหมือนรายได้ปกติ จนกว่าจะมี chargeback และเรื่องร้องเรียนจากลูกค้า ถ้าทีม fraud กับทีม security ดูคนละ dashboard ช่องว่างระหว่างสองทีมนี้คือจุดที่เรื่องนี้เกิด


  
  
  "Nothing is broken. That's the problem."



"Nothing is broken. That's the problem.": business logic abuse

สไลด์ที่สองที่ผมจะเอาไปเสนอบอร์ดคือเรื่อง business logic abuse มีตัวอย่าง 3 แบบ


Parameter tampering: แก้ amount: 10 เป็น amount: 1000 ใน POST /api/transfer ที่แอปเชื่อถือค่านั้น
Sequence abuse: ข้ามขั้น Approve ในลำดับ Submit, Verify, Approve, Receive
Scraping: ดูดราคา ข้อเสนอ และข้อมูลลูกค้าด้วยความเร็วระดับเครื่อง


ไม่มี CVE ไม่มี exploit payload ไม่มี alarm ทุก request เป็น API call ที่ถูกต้อง สไลด์สรุปเองว่า valid API กำลังถูกใช้ทำร้ายคุณ

มุมเทคนิค นี่คือกลุ่มปัญหาที่ scanner และ WAF แบบ signature (รวมชุด rule ตาม OWASP Top 10) มักมองข้าม เพราะ request รูปแบบถูกต้อง ช่องโหว่อยู่ที่กฎทางธุรกิจ การหาต้องอาศัยคนที่เข้าใจ workflow แล้วถามว่าถ้าข้ามหรือทำซ้ำขั้นตอนนี้จะเกิดอะไร การวิเคราะห์พฤติกรรม API ตอน runtime ช่วยได้ แต่ design review และ server-side validation ยังเป็นด่านแรก

ความหมายต่อธุรกิจ รายงาน penetration test ของคุณอาจสะอาด แล้วคุณก็ยังเสียเงินด้วยวิธีนี้ได้ ลองถามว่าการทดสอบรอบล่าสุดครอบคลุมการใช้ business flow ในทางที่ผิดหรือเปล่า หรือสแกนช่องโหว่อย่างเดียว


  
  
  สามคำถามที่ Radware บอกว่าผู้ดูแลความปลอดภัยทุกคนควรตอบได้



สามคำถามที่ผู้ดูแลความปลอดภัยทุกคนควรตอบได้


ก่อน go-live: รู้จักทุก API และ AI agent ที่เปิดออกไปหรือไม่ รวมถึงตัวที่ไม่มีใครจดไว้
ตอน production: ใครป้องกัน API และ agent เหล่านั้นขณะที่ลูกค้า แอป และ AI agent เรียกใช้อยู่
ตามเวลา: ติดตามพฤติกรรมและให้คะแนนความเสี่ยงที่เปลี่ยนไปได้อย่างไร


เกณฑ์ของสไลด์คือ ถ้าคำตอบขึ้นต้นด้วย "I think so" แสดงว่าเจอช่องโหว่แล้ว

ผมคิดว่านี่คือสิ่งที่มีประโยชน์ที่สุดในทั้งเด็ค เพราะไม่มีต้นทุนและใช้ได้กับทุกผู้ขาย ลองถามคำถามเหล่านี้กับหัวหน้าทีม security ของคุณ คำตอบข้อแรกตามจริงมักเป็นสเปรดชีตที่ไม่ได้อัปเดตมานาน


  
  
  ครึ่งหลัง: AI agent เป็น attack surface ใหม่



Enabling AI business initiatives securely (Radware Agentic AI Solution)


Solution architecture ระดับสูง: approved agents กับ shadow AI


Agentic AI protection ต้องมี runtime security

สไลด์ช่วงหลังเข้าเรื่องที่ Radware เรียกว่า Agentic AI solution ตามที่นำเสนอมีดังนี้


policy enforcer ที่ discover, classify, enforce และ monitor AI agent
การแบ่ง agent ที่องค์กรอนุมัติ (ตัวที่เขียนเอง เครื่องมือ dev บน desktop และแพลตฟอร์มอย่าง Teams, Slack) กับ "shadow AI" ที่ไม่มีใครอนุมัติ (แอปบนเครื่อง และ browser extension)
การแมปกับมาตรฐานกำกับดูแล ได้แก่ EU AI Act, GDPR, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001 และอื่นๆ
ข้อเสนอว่าการป้องกัน agent ต้องมี runtime security สองชั้น ระดับ agent ตรวจจับ misuse, prompt injection และ tool abuse แบบ real time ระดับ LLM มี policy module ปรับได้ ครอบคลุม prompt ข้อมูลและ privacy content safety ไฟล์แนบ และการใช้ทรัพยากร
เส้นทาง traffic: Internet, DDoS, firewall, WAF, bot management, LLM guardrails แล้วถึง agent ที่มี behavioural layer


มุมเทคนิค ผมชอบที่วาดเป็นส่วนต่อขยายของเส้นทาง traffic เดิม แทนที่จะเป็นผลิตภัณฑ์ AI แยกอีกตัว ส่วนที่ผมระวังคือ behavioural layer ของ agent ใหม่และพิสูจน์น้อยที่สุด สไลด์ไม่มีตัวเลข detection rate หรือ false positive ถ้าจะประเมิน ให้ขอ proof of concept กับ agent ของตัวเอง แล้ววัดผลเอง

ความหมายต่อธุรกิจ พนักงานใช้เครื่องมือ AI ที่ IT ไม่ได้อนุมัติอยู่แล้ว ความเสี่ยงไม่ได้อยู่ที่ตัวเครื่องมือ แต่อยู่ที่ agent ทำงานด้วยสิทธิ์ของคนได้ ดังนั้น prompt injection ที่สำเร็จครั้งเดียวกลายเป็นการกระทำที่ได้รับอนุญาต ต้องมี inventory ของ agent เหมือนที่มี inventory ของโน้ตบุ๊ก


  
  
  ถ้าจะลงมือวันจันทร์



ถามหัวหน้าทีม security ด้วยสามคำถามข้างบน แล้วจดคำตอบจริง
ถามเจ้าของ API ว่า business flow ไหนข้ามหรือทำซ้ำได้ และใครเคยทดสอบ

ถ้าจะประเมิน behavioural detection ให้รันบน traffic ของตัวเองและตัดสินอัตรา false positive เอง

title: Reaproveitando Smartphones Antigos como Servidores de IA de Borda com Linux (PostmarketOS / ARM64)
title_hi: Reaproveitando Smartphones Antigos como Servidores de IA de Borda com Linux (PostmarketOS / ARM64)
summary: A maioria dos desenvolvedores e entusiastas de hardware possui algum smartphone antigo esquecido em uma gaveta. Celulare
content:
A maioria dos desenvolvedores e entusiastas de hardware possui algum smartphone antigo esquecido em uma gaveta. Celulares topo de linha de gerações passadas (como os equipados com Snapdragon 845 ou Snapdragon 870) possuem:


6GB a 8GB de memória LPDDR4X rápida;
SoCs Octa-Core de 64 bits com excelente eficiência por Watt;
Armazenamento flash UFS veloz;

Uma bateria integrada (UPS/No-break nativo) que impede o desligamento súbito em caso de queda de energia.


Enquanto rodar ferramentas no Android via Termux frequentemente sofre com o OOM killer agressivo do sistema operacional móvel, instalar uma distribuição Linux real como o postmarketOS (baseado no Alpine Linux) transforma o celular em um micro-servidor bare-metal de baixo consumo.

Neste artigo, veremos como configurar um nó de inferência de IA local (Edge AI) rodando Ollama e Small Language Models (SLMs) diretamente no hardware ARM64.





  
  
  1. Por que postmarketOS em vez de Android/Termux?





Aspecto
Android + Termux
postmarketOS (Alpine Linux)




Kernel
Kernel customizado do fabricante (antigo)
Kernel Linux mainline upstream


Overhead de RAM
~2.5GB consumidos pela JVM e serviços Android
Menos de 200MB de RAM em idle


Gerenciamento de Processos
Android suspende daemons em background
systemd / OpenRC padrão de servidor


Acesso a Pacotes
Repositórios limitados do Termux
Repositórios completos Alpine ARM64 (apk)








  
  
  2. Preparando o Ambiente Headless


Após flashear o postmarketOS no dispositivo (ex: Xiaomi Pocophone F1, OnePlus 6, etc.), o primeiro passo para maximizar a memória disponível para os modelos de IA é desativar a interface gráfica (Phosh ou Plasma Mobile) e mascarar a suspensão profunda:



# Conectado via SSH no aparelho
# 1. Desativar suspensão para não derrubar a conexão de rede
sudo systemctl mask sleep.target suspend.target hibernate.target hybrid-sleep.target

# 2. Desativar interface gráfica no boot (modo servidor puro)
sudo systemctl set-default multi-user.target






Após reiniciar, o sistema consumirá míseros 150MB a 200MB de RAM, deixando mais de 5.5GB livres para carregar pesos de modelos de linguagem diretamente na memória unificada do SoC.





  
  
  3. Instalando o Ollama no ARM64


O Ollama possui compilações oficiais compatíveis com a arquitetura aarch64. A instalação pode ser realizada via script oficial:



curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh






Para garantir que o serviço escute em todas as interfaces da sua rede local privada (ou na malha Tailscale), configure as variáveis de ambiente do serviço:



sudo systemctl edit ollama.service






Insira:



[Service]
Environment="OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0:11434"
Environment="OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=24h"






Reinicie o serviço:



sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart ollama.service










  
  
  4. Escolha e Benchmark de Modelos SLM para Edge


Em chips como o Snapdragon 845/870, modelos de 1B a 3B de parâmetros quantizados em 4 bits (GGUF) oferecem um equilíbrio ideal entre velocidade e consumo de memória:



# Modelo ultra-rápido para código e raciocínio lógico (consome ~1.2GB de RAM)
ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:1.5b

# Modelo excelente para conversação e triagem de tarefas gerais (consome ~2.1GB de RAM)
ollama pull llama3.2:3b







  
  
  Resultados de Performance (Snapdragon 845 / 6GB RAM):




Qwen 2.5 Coder 1.5B (Q4_K_M): ~12 a 15 tokens/segundo.

Llama 3.2 3B (Q4_K_M): ~7 a 9 tokens/segundo.

Consumo Energético: Menos de 3 Watts sob carga máxima de inferência.






  
  
  Conclusão e Recursos


Reaproveitar hardware existente reduz lixo eletrônico e oferece uma infraestrutura de IA privada 24/7 sem custos recorrentes em nuvem. Com a bateria interna do smartphone, você ganha ainda tolerância total contra oscilações de energia elétrica.

summary: I work part-time in a grocery store. Stocking shelves, facing product, the whole thing. One night I thought: what if I m
content:
I work part-time in a grocery store. Stocking shelves, facing product, the whole thing. One night I thought: what if I made that into a game? So my team and I did. It's called STOCK BOY - a 16-bit grocery rush game, and it's the flagship of my little studio, Levi Studios.

You clock in. Customers walk in with a list. You tap them and serve from your shelves. Empty shelves mean angry walkouts. Then the lunch rush hits and it gets wild.

But here's the part I'm proud of, and the reason I'm writing this:

The client holds no stock. None.

The stock is packed by bots (we call them academy residents - they're learning tools, named and credited, never mistaken for people), and every crate is stamped with the name of the bot that packed it. The ledger lives on the server. Scores get validated there too.

No box, no store. Literally - the game shows an honest STORE OPEN / STORE CLOSED sign driven by a real heartbeat from the server. If the box is down, the sign says closed. I don't fake it.

Why build it this way? Because I wanted one economy. Bot work becomes crates, crates become what players sell, scores and trophies flow back to the server. The bots' work and the players' work live in the same world. Mixing worlds, I call it.

It's also just... mine. The whole thing runs on that $60 box - the game server, the chat, the score authority, the mint. If your build can't run on the cheapest machine you own, it's too big. That's my rule.
